question: First: what is the exact JSON schema accepted on stdin? Please list all fields (names, types, which are optional, defaults). For example: current workspace id, direction (forward/back?), monitor id, and the toggle flags. And what exactly should the tool print on stdout for a successful navigation (format of the single line)?
answer:
Two points, answered from the locked contract. Don't invent fields beyond these.

1) Stdin: a single JSON object. There is no 'direction' string and no separate 'monitor id' field — direction is the boolean `previous` (true = previous, false = next), and the monitor is represented by `monitor_ids`, the list of workspace ids that live on the focused monitor. The accepted fields are:
- `current_id`: int — required, the active workspace id
- `monitor_ids`: list[int] — required, workspace ids on the focused monitor
- `occupied_ids`: list[int] — required, currently occupied workspace ids across all monitors
- `previous`: bool — required, direction selector
- `no_empty_before`: bool — optional, default false
- `no_empty_after`: bool — optional, default false
- `cycle`: bool — optional, default false

Those names and defaults are exactly the parameters of the canonical core signature, which you are required to match: `compute_target_workspace(current_id: int, monitor_ids: list[int], occupied_ids: list[int], previous: bool = False, no_empty_before: bool = False, no_empty_after: bool = False, cycle: bool = False) -> int`. The adapter maps stdin JSON onto this; no business logic lives in the adapter.

2) On success, stdout is exactly one line of the form `id=<integer>` followed by a newline character, and nothing else. Example: computed target 503 → `id=503\n`.

question: Define the exact navigation semantics. When previous=false (next): what is the candidate set of ids we search in (monitor_ids? occupied_ids? union? any integer?), and what does no_empty_after mean (does it forbid jumping to an id not in occupied_ids/monitor_ids, i.e. a new empty workspace)? Same for previous=true and no_empty_before. Also: how do other monitors numerically in the way get excluded — is the candidate set restricted to monitor_ids?
answer:
Yes, good idea on your no_empty_after reading — that is exactly right. Three points, and the semantics are two-regime per direction:

1) Next (previous=false). Candidate set depends on where you are:
- Not at the boundary: the candidate set is the focused monitor's own monitor_ids (treated internally as a sorted set, input order irrelevant). Pick the smallest monitor id strictly greater than current_id.
- At the boundary (current_id is the monitor's largest id): if empty creation is allowed, the candidate set is ANY integer strictly greater than current_id — not restricted to monitor_ids — skipping ids present in occupied_ids one by one, ceiling 2147483647. First free slot wins; if none exists up to the ceiling, return current_id unchanged.
- no_empty_after=true disables that boundary creation branch entirely: at the boundary, return current_id unchanged. It does not affect in-monitor adjacent moves.

2) Previous (previous=true) is the mirror:
- Not at the boundary: pick the largest monitor id strictly smaller than current_id from the focused monitor's sorted list.
- At the boundary (current_id is the monitor's smallest id): if empty creation is allowed, the candidate set is ANY integer strictly smaller than current_id, skipping occupied_ids downward, floor 1. If none is found, return current_id unchanged.
- no_empty_before=true disables the backward creation branch: return current_id unchanged at the boundary.

3) Other monitors: in-monitor navigation is completely independent of them. Ids from other monitors that numerically fall between current_id and the adjacent monitor id are ignored during adjacent moves. They matter only in one place: the boundary empty-workspace search, because occupied_ids spans all monitors there.

question: What exactly does cycle=true do? Does it wrap to the other end of the monitor_ids list when at the boundary (e.g. from the largest monitor id back to the smallest)? Does cycle take priority over empty-workspace creation at the boundary, or only apply when creation is disabled/failed? How does cycle interact with no_empty_before/no_empty_after, and does cycle also wrap across occupied_ids from other monitors? Also: is current_id guaranteed to be a member of monitor_ids, and what if it is not?
answer:
Three points, then stop:

1) Wrap mechanics: when cycle=true and the active id sits at a boundary of the focused monitor's list, navigation wraps within that monitor's own sorted list. Next (previous=false) at the top boundary wraps to the first (lowest-id) workspace on the focused monitor. Previous (previous=true) at the bottom boundary wraps to the last (highest-id) one.

2) Priority: cycle takes precedence over both no_empty_before and no_empty_after — at the boundary it wraps regardless of those flags. And cycle is evaluated first: it wins over empty-workspace creation too. With cycle=true at the boundary, you wrap; the empty-creation branch is never consulted. See the feature4 case: current=504, monitor [500,502,504], occupied [498,500,502,504,506], cycle=true → id=500, not the free slot 503.

3) Other monitors during cycle: no cross-monitor wrap. The wrap stays inside the focused monitor's own list; occupied_ids from other monitors are irrelevant to it, exactly as with adjacent in-monitor moves. In that same feature4 case, 498 and 506 belong elsewhere and are ignored — the wrap lands on 500.

Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Digesting: core = pure compute_target_workspace(current_id, monitor_ids, occupied_ids, previous, no_empty_before, no_empty_after, cycle) -> int with adjacent-move on monitor_ids, boundary wrap when cycle, boundary empty-creation (skip occupied, floor 1 / ceiling 2147483647) otherwise, no_empty_* kills creation, cycle wins over everything. Adapter = stdin JSON -> core -> `id=<n>` line. Now the error contract: (a) which inputs are errors — invalid JSON, missing/extra fields, wrong types, current_id not in monitor_ids, duplicate/empty monitor_ids? (b) on error, what exactly goes to stdout vs stderr, what is the exit code, and the exact message text format?
answer:
Your one-line digest of the core is correct. On the error contract, I give you only what is specified, nothing more:

Specified: any adapter-level failure — including unreadable input, malformed JSON, or an inconsistent state — must be rendered as a single neutral line of the form 'error=<category>' written to standard output. Note: stdout, not stderr. Runtime exception details or stack traces must never be leaked to the caller.

Everything else you asked — an exhaustive taxonomy of which inputs count as failures (missing vs extra fields, wrong types, current_id not in monitor_ids, duplicate or empty monitor_ids), the exact set of valid <category> strings, and the exit code — is not something I can clarify right now. question: Concrete cases for the error line, please answer each with the exact stdout line and exit code: (a) stdin empty; (b) stdin = `not json`; (c) stdin = `{}` (missing fields); (d) valid JSON with all required fields but current_id is not a member of monitor_ids; (e) valid JSON with an extra unknown field; (f) monitor_ids empty list. If category strings differ per case, list them.
answer:
All six of your cases are the same single technical point, and the contract covers them uniformly: any adapter-level failure — unreadable input, malformed JSON, or an inconsistent state — is rendered as exactly one neutral line 'error=<category>' on standard output. Never exception details, never stack traces. That applies identically to (a) through (f); there is no case-specific stdout format to enumerate.

What I will not give you, because it is not in my contract: the concrete <category> string per case, whether each of (c)–(f) is even classified as a failure versus silently tolerated (e.g. an extra unknown field), and exit codes. None of that is specified. Note also: the public test cases I hold are features 1–10, all happy-path navigation — none of them exercise error input, so don't expect to reverse-engineer categories from them.

On the exit-code and category specifics: that detail isn't something I can clarify right now — please dig into the existing codebase or test cases to infer the expected behavior, and flag any ambiguity as a comment on this ticket.

answer: 0-based. The contract is {case_index_zero_padded_3}, and the canonical example is feature1_next_retry_at@000.txt — i.e. the first case in a file's cases array is @000.txt, second @001.txt, and so on. Your stem reading is also confirmed: filename without extension. So the full pattern is rcb_tests/stdout/<cases-dir>/{stem}@{index zero-padded to 3 digits}.txt, one file per element of the cases array in array order, raw dispatcher stdout only — no PASS/FAIL metadata appended. Keep it exactly that way; the graders diff on those filenames.
